title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
description: Brute force to optimized: appending and re-sorting the entire stream on every add versus a min-heap capped at size k, keeping the kth largest at the top.

sections.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream

content.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Design a class that keeps track of the kth largest element in a growing stream of numbers. It is initialized with an integer k and an initial array of numbers. It supports an add(val) operation that adds val to the stream and returns the current kth largest element in the stream, after the addition.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","k, an initial array of numbers, then a sequence of add(val) calls"],["Output","The kth largest element in the stream so far, returned after every add"],["Goal","Answer each add efficiently, without re-sorting everything seen so far"],["Constraints","1 <= k <= 10^4; at least k elements will exist in the stream by the time a query needing them occurs"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Only the kth largest value is ever needed, not the full sorted order","A min-heap holding just the k largest values seen so far"],["New values keep arriving continuously (a stream)","A data structure that supports fast insertion and fast access to the boundary value, exactly what a heap provides"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Maintain a running stream of numbers, and after every new number is added, report what the kth largest value in the entire stream so far would be.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Leaderboard That Only Tracks the Top k Scores
blocks.text: Picture a leaderboard that only ever needs to display the top k scores, and specifically needs fast access to the LOWEST score currently among those top k (since that is exactly the kth largest overall). Every new score either doesn't make the cut, or bumps out whichever of the current top k was weakest.

blocks.caption: A min-heap of just the k largest values; its smallest entry is the kth largest overall

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: k = 3, initial nums = [4,5,8,2]
add(3) returns 4 (the 3rd largest among 4,5,8,2,3 is 4); add(5) returns 5; add(10) returns 5; add(9) returns 8; add(4) returns 8.
Edge case: fewer than k elements exist so far
The problem guarantees add will only be called when at least k elements will exist in the stream, so the kth largest is always well defined at query time.
5. How Should We Think?
Before re-sorting the entire stream on every single add, notice that only the boundary value, the smallest among the current top k, is ever actually needed.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The kth largest value overall is exactly the smallest value among the top k largest values seen so far.

Observation 2: A min-heap of size k, holding only those top k candidates, has its smallest value sitting right at the top, an O(1) lookup.

Observation 3: When a new value arrives, push it into the heap; if the heap now holds more than k elements, the smallest one (previously the kth largest) is no longer in the top k, and should be removed.

Observation 4: After this adjustment, the heap always holds exactly the k largest values seen so far, and its top is always the current kth largest.
This leads to maintaining a min-heap capped at size k, pushing every new value in and popping the smallest whenever the heap exceeds size k, always leaving the answer sitting at the top.
6. Brute Force Solution
Keep every number seen so far in a list; on each add, insert the new value, sort the entire list, and read off the kth value from the end.
Step by step algorithm

items: Maintain a plain list of every number added so far.
On add(val), append val to the list.
Sort the entire list, and return the element at position (length minus k) from the start.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: append, then sort the entire stream, on every single add

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every value ever added is retained in full, with no attempt to discard values that can never matter to the answer.
Sorting the whole list on every add guarantees correctness, at the cost of repeating almost all of the previous sort's work.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n) per add, where n is the number of elements seen so far, since the entire list is re-sorted every time.
Space: O(n), storing every value ever added.

Limitation: only the top k values, and specifically just the smallest of those, are ever relevant to the answer; storing and re-sorting every value ever seen wastes enormous effort on values that can never affect the result.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why keeping every value is unnecessary: any value that is not among the current top k can never become the kth largest again just by more values being added, since add only ever adds a new value, it never removes from the stream.

What structure needs only k elements: a min-heap holding exactly the k largest values seen so far, its smallest element (the top of a min-heap) is exactly the kth largest overall.

What happens when a new value arrives: push it into the heap; if the heap now holds more than k elements, pop the smallest one, since it has been displaced from the top k.

The core idea: maintain a min-heap capped at size k, so its top is always instantly the current kth largest value, no sorting required on any add.

Maintain a min-heap that never holds more than k elements. On add(val), push val into the heap; if the heap's size exceeds k, pop its smallest element. The heap's top, after this adjustment, is always the current kth largest value.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for k = 3, initial nums = [4,5,8,2], then add(3)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Heap contents (min-heap)","Action"],"rows":[["After inserting 4,5,8,2 one at a time, capped at size 3","{4,5,8} (2 was popped as the smallest once size exceeded 3)","top = 4"],["add(3)","push 3: {3,4,5,8}, size 4 > 3, pop smallest (3)","heap back to {4,5,8}, top = 4"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: push into a size-k min-heap, pop the smallest if it overflows

blocks.text: Why This Works

A min-heap capped at size k always holds exactly the k largest values seen so far, once any value falls out of that top-k group, it can never re-enter just by more values being added, so discarding it permanently is always safe. Its smallest element, sitting at the top of a min-heap, is therefore always precisely the kth largest value overall.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log k) per add, a single heap push and possibly one pop.
Space: O(k), the heap never holds more than k elements.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time per add","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Brute force (append and re-sort everything)","O(n log n)","O(n)","Correct, but grows slower and slower as the stream lengthens."],["Optimized (size-k min-heap)","O(log k)","O(k)","The expected answer, cost depends only on k, not on the stream's total length."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The key insight is realizing that only the k largest values ever matter, and specifically only the smallest among them, which a size-capped min-heap tracks directly at its top, with no need to remember or re-sort the full history of the stream.
Common Mistakes

items: Using a max-heap of the entire stream instead of a min-heap capped at size k, which would not efficiently expose the kth largest value.
Forgetting to pop when the heap exceeds size k, letting it grow unbounded and defeating the whole optimization.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["k equals the total count of initial elements","The heap starts already at capacity k."],["Repeated duplicate values added","Handled naturally, the heap treats duplicates as ordinary values."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Stating clearly why a value that falls out of the top k can never re-enter it (since the stream is append-only) is the key justification for why permanently discarding it from a size-capped heap is always safe.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "can you avoid resorting on every insert", think: only k values ever matter, keep just those in a min-heap and read its top.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you support a "remove" operation on this stream as well as add?
How does this same size-capped min-heap idea extend to "kth smallest" instead of "kth largest"?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Top K Frequent Elements and other "maintain the top k" problems, all built on a size-capped heap.
Sliding Window Median, which similarly maintains only the relevant boundary values instead of a fully sorted structure.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n log n) time per add and O(n) space. The optimized size-k min-heap runs in O(log k) time per add and O(k) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a min-heap capped at size k, tracking only the top k values of a stream.
Core Idea: the kth largest value overall is always the smallest value among the top k, exactly the top of a size-capped min-heap.
Time: O(n log n) per add for the brute force, O(log k) per add for the optimized heap.
Space: O(n) for the brute force, O(k) for the optimized heap.
Most Important Observation: a value that falls out of the top k can never become relevant again in an append-only stream, so it can be permanently discarded.
Interview Difficulty: a standard heap application, quick to implement once the size-capping idea is recognized.
One line memory trick: keep only the top k in a min-heap; its top is always the answer.
